pos: n. (craft; cunning management; in the Authorized Version, statecraft turned to deceit)
etymology: From Greek politeia, the conduct of civil affairs, through Latin politia and Old French policie. English narrowed the sense from the plain art of governing to the crooked art of getting one's way by it — the sense Daniel uses.
biblical_def:
Daniel's eighth chapter closes its vision of the little horn with one sentence that has become the standard description of the last enemy's method: through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand. The verse follows two others describing raw power — a king of fierce countenance, mighty but not by his own power, who destroys wonderfully and prospers and practises. Policy is what such power does once it has learned that force alone invites resistance. It is intelligence bent to a bad end: the same faculty Scripture elsewhere calls prudence or understanding, but aimed at prospering craft instead of prospering righteousness.

The Hebrew word behind policy is the ordinary noun for insight or discretion — the very word used elsewhere of the wisdom Solomon asked for and God gave. Daniel's irony is exact: the last tyrant is not a fool. He has real understanding, real strategic gift, and he spends the whole of it magnifying himself and standing against the Prince of princes. And the chapter's last line refuses the tyrant even the dignity of a worthy end — he shall be broken without hand, undone by no human weapon at all. Policy that serves craft can prosper for a season and cannot, in the end, prosper against God; the same insight that built the throne cannot buy off the sentence already written against it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the art or manner of governing a nation; also, art, prudence, or dexterity in management, often with the sense of cunning or artifice.
webster_full: POLICY, n. The art or manner of governing a state; also, stratagem, cunning management, artifice.
CRAFT, n. Art, skill, dexterity; also cunning, artifice, guile employed to effect a purpose.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to thrive; to grow or increase in wealth, favor or power.
MAGNIFY, v.t. To make great or greater; to exalt or extol; to enlarge in representation, whether by praise or by pride.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; a ruler of a nation or territory; one of the highest civil rank.
scriptures: Dan 8:23
And in the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors are come to the full, a king of fierce countenance, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
Dan 8:24
And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power: and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people.
Dan 8:25

And through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and by peace shall destroy many: he shall also stand up against the Prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand.
There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD.
corruption_summary: Policy is treated as morally neutral savvy — whatever works — when Daniel uses the word precisely to name insight that has been bent to serve deceit.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage keeps policy almost entirely in the neutral sense Webster gave it first — a company's policy, a government's policy, the plain art of governing. Daniel's use is the second, darker sense: intelligence in the service of craft, understanding aimed not at truth but at advantage. It is not stupidity dressed up; it is real gift, real strategic depth, spent on an end that will not stand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it does face the older and steadier temptation the word always carried: the assumption that if a policy prospers it must be wise, and that success is its own vindication. Daniel's little horn prospers for a set season and by a set craft, and is broken at the end without any hand at all — the pattern is meant to be read backward from that ending, not forward from the momentary success. The insight a man has is never sufficient warrant for the use he puts it to.
roots_summary: Hebrew sekel (H7922), insight or discretion, used ironically of the tyrant's craft; mirmah (H4820), deceit, the craft he causes to prosper.
roots_lines: Hebrew sekel (H7922) — insight, discretion, understanding; the same faculty Solomon asked for, here bent to a false end.
Hebrew mirmah (H4820) — deceit, treachery, guile; the “craft” that policy causes to prosper.
Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow great, to magnify; the tyrant's own heart is the subject.
Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, to shatter; his end, and “without hand” at that.
Hebrew sar (H8269) — a prince, chief, ruler; here the title of the one power his policy cannot touch.
usage: “through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand” — Daniel's summary of the last tyrant's method.
“he shall also stand up against the Prince of princes” — the true scale of the ambition policy serves.
“but he shall be broken without hand” — the end no policy can prevent.

pos: n. (a body of elders or rulers; in the Authorized Version, the eldership of Israel gathered with the Sanhedrin)
etymology: Latin senatus, from senex, an old man — a council of elders, the same root that gives senior and senile. The Authorized Version uses it once, translating a Greek word for the same idea of gathered eldership.
biblical_def:
Acts five records the second arrest of the apostles, and Luke is careful to specify exactly who assembled against them: the high priest came, and they that were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel. Two bodies are named side by side — the council, meaning the Sanhedrin proper, and the senate, the wider eldership of the nation, as if Luke wants no reader to imagine this was a small or hasty proceeding. The full civil and religious authority of Israel convened to deal with a dozen fishermen and a formerly persecuting Pharisee.

What follows is the real point of the word's one appearance. This senate, gathered in its fullest strength, sends for the apostles — and finds the prison empty and the guards baffled, because an angel of the Lord had opened the doors by night. When the apostles are found preaching in the temple exactly where they had been forbidden, and brought again before this same senate, Peter gives the answer that outlives every session of it: we ought to obey God rather than men. The senate of Israel, however weighty its assembly, is shown deliberating over men whom God had already released; Gamaliel, one of its own number, is the one who tells it so. A council can be entirely legitimate in form and still be entirely wrong about who is actually in charge of the prison.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an assembly or council of counselors of a state, particularly one composed of aged men, or those of the highest wisdom or dignity in a nation.
webster_full: SENATE, n. An assembly or council of counselors of state; a body of men appointed or elected to represent a state or a district in the government.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men called together for consultation, deliberation, or advice.
ELDER, n. A person who, on account of his age, has authority or precedence; also, an officer in the church.
APOSTLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; in the New Testament, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel.
OBEY, v.t. To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior, or with the requirements of law, moral, political or municipal.
scriptures: Act 5:21

And when they heard that, they entered into the temple early in the morning, and taught. But the high priest came, and they that were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 5:34
Then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles forth a little space;

And the LORD said unto Moses, Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they may stand there with thee.
corruption_summary: A senate's weight of numbers and age is taken for the weight of truth, when Acts sets the full assembled senate of Israel directly against an angel who has already emptied its prison.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition — a senate is still understood as an assembled body of counselors, much as Webster defined it. The principle to recover is older than any modern controversy: the size, age, and legitimacy of a deliberative body is no guarantee that its deliberation is right. Israel's senate, gathered in full and formal strength, was at that very hour opposing men God had already vindicated by an empty prison and an open door.

Gamaliel, sitting within that senate, is the one who counsels caution — if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it — and the caution is itself an admission that the senate's own judgment is not the final court. Peter's answer to the whole body, we ought to obey God rather than men, does not despise lawful authority; it simply refuses to let any senate, however constituted, stand in the seat that belongs to God alone.
roots_summary: Greek gerousia (G1087), the senate or council of elders; sunedrion (G4892), the council, the Sanhedrin named alongside it.
roots_lines: Greek gerousia (G1087) — a senate, an assembly of elders; from geron, an old man, the same idea as the Latin root.
Greek sunedrion (G4892) — a council, a sitting-together; the Sanhedrin, named beside the senate in the same verse.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder; the ordinary word for the office both bodies represented.
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; the verb behind Peter's answer, We ought to obey God.
Hebrew zaqen (H2205) — an elder, an old man; the standing Old Testament office the senate of Israel continued.
usage: “called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel” — the full assembled authority of the nation.
“we ought to obey God rather than men” — the apostles' answer to that assembly.
“if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” — Gamaliel's own warning to the senate he sat in.

pos: n. (freedom from care or danger; also, a pledge or bond given to guarantee performance)
etymology: Latin securitas, from se-, without, and cura, care — the same root as cure and curious. The word carries both senses Webster still lists: the inward freedom from anxiety, and the outward legal bond that guarantees it.
biblical_def:
Luke's one use of the word in Acts is entirely legal, and easy to miss on a fast reading. When the Thessalonian mob cannot find Paul, they drag Jason before the rulers instead, and the city officials, unable to hold anyone on the actual charge, settle for taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go — a bond, almost certainly a sum of money, guaranteeing that no more trouble would come of the matter and that Paul would move on. It is the ordinary machinery of Roman civic order, and Luke records it without comment, one more small true detail in a book full of them.

The larger biblical use of the English word, though never in this exact form, is the false peace Paul warns of in Thessalonians: when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them. Jason's security was a real, working, legal guarantee within its limits — a bond that actually did what it promised. The security the world offers itself against the day of the Lord is the opposite: a felt safety with no bond behind it at all, spoken exactly when the danger is nearest. Scripture never condemns the ordinary bonds of civil life that Jason's case shows working as intended; it condemns the far more dangerous habit of mistaking a feeling of safety for a covenant that actually holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): freedom from fear, anxiety or care; also, a pledge, surety, or bond given as a guarantee for the performance of a contract or the payment of a debt.
webster_full: SECURITY, n. Protection; freedom from danger; also, that which secures or guarantees, as a pledge, surety or bond.
SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger; exemption from hurt, injury or loss.
PLEDGE, n. A pawn; something given or deposited as security for the performance of some act.
SUDDEN, a. Happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly; hasty.
DWELL, v.i. To abide as a permanent resident; to have a fixed residence; to live in safety and quiet.
scriptures: Act 17:9
And when they had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go.
For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
But when ye go over Jordan, and dwell in the land which the LORD your God giveth you to inherit, and when he giveth you rest from all your enemies round about, so that ye dwell in safety;
corruption_summary: Security is sold as a feeling to be purchased or generated, when Scripture treats real security as either a specific bond that actually holds or the LORD's own keeping — and treats felt safety without either as the most dangerous state a man can be in.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the legal sense Jason's case shows — a bond is still a bond. The principle worth recovering is Paul's, in the very next breath of Thessalonians: the world's Peace and safety is spoken loudest immediately before sudden destruction, precisely because it is a feeling manufactured without the bond of a covenant behind it.

David's security in the fourth Psalm has the opposite structure entirely — he lays himself down and sleeps not because circumstances are safe but because the LORD, and the LORD only, makes him dwell in safety. That is security with an actual guarantor named, exactly as Jason's bond named an actual guarantor. The false security condemned in Thessalonians is not confidence as such; it is confidence with the guarantor left out, felt safety mistaken for a promise no one actually made.
roots_summary: Greek hikanos (G2425), sufficient, behind the legal bond taken of Jason; asphaleia (G803), safety, security, the word Paul quotes as the world's false cry.
roots_lines: Greek hikanos (G2425) — sufficient, enough; the term behind “security,” a sufficient bond or guarantee taken of Jason.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — safety, security, certainty; the very word the world cries in 1 Thessalonians 5:3.
Greek aiphnidios (G160) — sudden, unforeseen; the destruction that answers that false cry.
Hebrew betach (H983) — safety, security, confidence; the dwelling David describes in Psalm 4:8 and Deuteronomy 12:10.
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down; David's own posture of rest, grounded in the LORD alone.
usage: “when they had taken security of Jason” — the ordinary bond of Roman civic order.
“when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh” — the false security Paul warns of.
“thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” — the true security, and its only guarantor.

pos: n. (a term or stipulation on which an agreement rests; also, one's state or rank)
etymology: Latin condicio, from con-, together, and dicere, to say — a thing spoken together, agreed upon in advance. The word arrives in the Authorized Version wherever a covenant, a treaty, or a bargain has terms attached to it.
biblical_def:
Scripture's two clearest uses of condition sit at opposite ends of the same idea, and together they show what the word actually does in the text: it names the stated term on which a covenant of peace, or a covenant of destruction, will be granted. Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers terms with the coldest possible condition attached — a covenant purchased only by the thrusting out of every right eye in the city, a reproach laid deliberately upon Israel. Saul's deliverance of Jabesh-gilead is his first great act as king precisely because he refuses to let that condition stand.

Christ's own use of the word, in the parable of the king going to war, describes the ordinary business of any commander facing an enemy twice his strength: while the stronger king is still a great way off, he sends an ambassage and desireth conditions of peace. The parable is about counting the cost of discipleship, and the condition it names is real — a settlement is possible, but only on stated terms, sought while there is still time to seek them. Between Nahash's condition and the parable's, Scripture draws the line believers are meant to see: some terms are offered by an enemy who means only shame, and some conditions of peace are offered in good faith while the door is still open, and wisdom lies in telling which is which before the terms are forced upon you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a term or stipulation on which a promise, contract or grant is made to depend; also, state, situation, or rank.
webster_full: CONDITION, n. A term of a contract; a provision on which the rest of an agreement depends; also, state, external circumstances.
COVENANT, n. A mutual agreement of two or more persons or parties, in writing, and under seal.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious language; shame; disgrace.
AMBASSAGE, n. A message or errand sent by an ambassador; the business intrusted to a public minister.
DESIRE, v.t. To wish; to long for the possession or enjoyment of, with a proportionate degree of pleasure in the anticipation.
scriptures: And Nahash the Ammonite answered them, On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may thrust out all your right eyes, and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel.
Then Nahash the Ammonite came up, and encamped against Jabeshgilead: and all the men of Jabesh said unto Nahash, Make a covenant with us, and we will serve thee.
Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.
corruption_summary: Every stated condition is treated as a negotiating tactic to be gamed, when Scripture uses the word to expose the real character of the one setting it — whether an enemy offering shame or a king still willing to make peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; contracts still rest on stated conditions. The principle worth recovering is that the same word covers both Nahash's condition and Christ's parable of the king seeking peace, and the difference between them is not the form of the word but the will behind it.

Nahash's condition was never a genuine basis for covenant at all — it was a demand for humiliation dressed as an offer of terms, and Saul's answer to it, sending pieces of oxen throughout Israel to summon an army, treated it exactly so. The king in Luke's parable, by contrast, seeks conditions of peace in good faith while the stronger force is still a great way off. The task Scripture actually sets before a reader is not suspicion of every condition as such, but the discernment to know, before the terms are forced upon him, which kind of covenant he is being offered.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant, the standing term behind every condition named in the Old Testament; Greek eirene (G1515), peace, the object of the conditions Christ's king seeks.
roots_lines: Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the term Nahash offers and Saul refuses to let stand on those conditions.
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; what Nahash's condition was actually designed to lay upon Israel.
Greek presbeia (G4242) — an ambassage, an embassy; the mission the weaker king sends while there is still time.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace; the object of the conditions the parable's king desires.
Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count, to calculate; the verb just before, of counting the cost, that frames the whole parable.
usage: “On this condition will I make a covenant with you” — Nahash's demand at Jabesh-gilead.
“he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace” — the weaker king in Christ's parable.
“Or what king, going to make war against another king” — the counting of the cost that the conditions answer.

pos: a. (belonging to oneself alone; not public; done apart from others)
etymology: Latin privatus, past participle of privare, to deprive, to set apart — a thing withdrawn from the common or public stock. What is private is, at root, what has been separated out from the general view.
biblical_def:
The Gospels use privately almost always of the disciples pulling Christ aside, away from the crowds that pressed on every side of His public ministry, to ask what they could not or would not ask in front of others. On the Mount of Olives, across from the temple, they come to Him privately to ask when the things He had just foretold would come to pass — and the whole Olivet discourse follows as His private answer to a private question. Elsewhere they ask privately why they could not cast out a particular demon, and are told plainly, in private, what public rebuke would only have shamed them to hear.

What emerges across these scenes is a real pattern of ministry, not merely a scheduling detail: Christ taught crowds in parables and taught His own disciples plainly, and the private setting was where the plain teaching happened. Peter's second epistle warns against a corruption of exactly this pattern — false teachers who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, using private access for the opposite purpose, smuggling error in where no crowd can hear it challenged. The private place in Scripture is not secrecy for its own sake; it is where Christ deepens what the crowd could not yet bear, and precisely for that reason it is also where a false teacher can do the most damage before anyone else notices.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): belonging to one person only, or to a few, in opposition to public; not open or in the presence of others; secret.
webster_full: PRIVATE, a. Sequestered from company or observation; not public; peculiar to one's self and family.
PRIVILY, adv. Privately; secretly; not openly or publicly.
DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives instruction from another, particularly an early follower of Christ.
REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprove; to check by reproof.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion, held and adhered to pertinaciously.
scriptures: Mat 24:3
And as he sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?
Mar 9:28
And when he was come into the house, his disciples asked him privately, Why could not we cast him out?
Mar 4:34
But without a parable spake he not unto them: and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
corruption_summary: Privacy is treated as an absolute right owed to the self against all correction, when the Gospels use private access chiefly as the place where Christ deepens hard teaching His disciples could not yet bear in public.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, but it does face a quiet inversion of its biblical use. In the Gospels, private access to Christ is where a disciple's honest question gets a fuller answer than the crowd received — it deepens accountability, it does not escape it. The disciples ask privately precisely so they can understand better, not so they can avoid being taught.

Peter's warning shows the same setting turned to the opposite purpose: false teachers who work privily, bringing in heresy where no one is positioned to challenge it before the damage is done. The lesson is not that private conversation is suspect — Christ Himself used it constantly and well — but that private access is a tool, and its worth depends entirely on whether it is used, as the disciples used it, to seek fuller truth, or, as Peter's false teachers used it, to smuggle in error unseen.
roots_summary: Greek idios (G2398), one's own, apart; the root behind the disciples' private questions and Christ's private teaching to His own.
roots_lines: Greek idios (G2398) — one's own, private, apart; the ordinary root behind “privately” in the Gospels.
Greek epilusis (G1955) — a loosing, an interpretation; Peter's word for what false private teaching wrongly claims for itself (2 Peter 1:20).
Greek pareisago (G3919) — to bring in secretly, alongside; the compound verb behind “privily shall bring in.”
Greek parabole (G3850) — a parable, a setting-beside; the public form of teaching private explanation completed.
Greek epiluo (G1956) — to explain fully, to expound; what Christ did for His disciples alone in Mark 4:34.
usage: “the disciples came unto him privately” — the setting of the Olivet discourse.
“when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples” — the pattern behind every private teaching.
“who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” — the same setting turned to a false use.

pos: a. (reciprocal; given and received in equal degree between two or more parties)
etymology: Latin mutuus, borrowed, exchanged, from mutare, to change — the same root that gives mutation and mutable. What is mutual has passed both ways, given by each to the other.
biblical_def:
Paul's one use of the word, at the close of his introduction to the Romans, is a small but telling correction of how he might have been read. He has just said he longs to see them, that he may impart some spiritual gift to establish them — language that, left there, could sound like an apostle arriving to hand down blessing from a superior height. He immediately corrects the impression: that is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me. The gift Paul brings is real, but the comfort he expects to receive back is just as real, and he names it before the sentence is finished.

The correction matters because it describes the actual shape of fellowship among believers who have never met. Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, writing to a church he did not found and had not yet visited, still expects to be comforted by their faith as much as they by his gift. Nothing in the passage suggests this mutuality erases the real difference between an apostle's calling and an ordinary believer's; it simply insists that the traffic runs both ways even so. A faith that only ever gives and never receives, or only ever receives and never gives, has missed something Paul was careful to name in his very first letter to a church he loved before he had ever stood in front of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): reciprocal; interchanged; given and received; acting in return, as mutual love, mutual advantage.
webster_full: MUTUAL, a. Reciprocal; interchanged, each acting in return or correspondence to the other; given and received.
IMPART, v.t. To grant; to bestow; to give a share or portion of something to another.
ESTABLISH, v.t. To settle firmly; to confirm; to fix or set beyond danger of overthrow or change.
COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind when depressed or enfeebled; to console; to give strength and hope.
FAITH, n. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity.
scriptures: Rom 1:11
For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established;
Rom 1:12
That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me.
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
Php 2:2
Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind.
corruption_summary: Mutual is flattened into mere sameness or equality of standing, when Paul uses it precisely across a real difference of calling — an apostle and an unmet church, each expecting to be comforted by the other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; mutual still means what Webster said, given and received on both sides. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own care in Romans 1: he does not let his real apostolic authority collapse the mutuality of faith between himself and the Romans, and he does not let the mutuality erase the real authority either. Both are true in the same two verses.

The same balance runs through his figure of the body in First Corinthians — members with genuinely different functions, none dispensable, all owing the same care one for another. Mutual comfort in the faith is not a claim that all callings are identical; it is a claim that no calling, however exalted, stands outside the ordinary traffic of giving and receiving that belongs to the whole body of Christ.
roots_summary: Greek allelon (G240), one another, the ordinary word behind reciprocal Christian duty; en allelois, the phrase underlying Paul's mutual comfort in Romans 1:12.
roots_lines: Greek allelon (G240) — one another, each other; the standing New Testament word for reciprocal duty among believers.
Greek sumparakaleo (G4837) — to comfort together with; Paul's compound verb in Romans 1:12, built from the same root as Comforter.
Greek meros (G3313) — a part, a member; the individual part owed care in 1 Corinthians 12:25.
Greek schisma (G4978) — a division, a schism; the tearing mutual care is meant to prevent.
Greek sumphonos (G4859) — sounding together, agreeing; the harmony Philippians 2:2 asks for as its shape.
usage: “that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me” — Paul's correction of his own opening words.
“that the members should have the same care one for another” — mutuality inside the figure of one body.
“being of one accord, of one mind” — the shared temper mutual faith is meant to produce.

pos: n. (a measured amount; magnitude or bulk considered as capable of increase or division)
etymology: Latin quantitas, from quantus, how much — a word built to answer exactly one question, how much of a thing there is. The Authorized Version's single use answers it about the smallest vessels in a great house.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's prophecy against Shebna the steward, and the raising up of Eliakim in his place, ends with an image that turns on the phrase vessels of small quantity. Eliakim is promised the key of the house of David, a peg fastened in a sure place, and every kind of household honor hung upon him — all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons. The picture is of an entire household's worth of dependents and possessions, down to the least cup, hung on one nail.

The verse that follows is the sober turn: that same nail, fastened in a sure place, will one day be removed, cut down, and fall, and everything hung upon it will be cut off. The vessel of small quantity is not condemned for being small — it is named precisely to show how much depends, great and small alike, on the one peg it is hung upon. A household's whole store, down to its least cup, rises or falls with the security of what it is fastened to; the word appears exactly once in Scripture, and it appears to make that one point unmistakable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the amount, bulk, or extent of any thing, as measured, or capable of being measured; a determinate or estimated amount.
webster_full: QUANTITY, n. That property of a thing which may be increased or diminished; bulk, weight, extent, or amount, considered without regard to quality.
VESSEL, n. A hollow utensil for holding liquors or other things; also, a ship or boat of any kind.
FASTEN, v.t. To fix firmly; to make fast; to attach securely to something.
GLORY, n. Splendor; magnificence; great beauty; also, honor, praise, and distinction.
REMOVE, v.t. To move from its place; to displace; to take away from a former position.
scriptures: And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house.
And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons.

In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the LORD hath spoken it.
The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
corruption_summary: Quantity is treated as morally weightless, a mere neutral measure, when Isaiah's one use of it sets every vessel great and small on the security of a single nail — the point of the word is dependence, not size.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; quantity still names sheer measured amount, as Webster gave it. The principle worth recovering from its one biblical appearance is that the word is used to gather up an entire household's worth of dependents, great vessels and small vessels alike, and show them all hanging on the strength of a single point of attachment.

The nail that bears the vessels of small quantity is later removed, cut down, and falls — and the burden with it. Eliakim's own weight of honor did not save the nail he was; what a peg is fastened to determines what happens to everything hung on it, however small. The lesson travels well past this one household: quantity of dependents, however great or small, is never itself the security — the fastening is.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatan (H6996), small, little; behind “small quantity,” describing the least vessels of the household hung on Eliakim's peg.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatan (H6996) — small, little, least; the adjective behind “small quantity” in Isaiah 22:24.
Hebrew keliy (H3627) — a vessel, an article, an implement; the ordinary word for the cups and flagons named here.
Hebrew yathed (H3489) — a nail, a peg, a pin; the fastening on which the whole household's honor hangs.
Hebrew maqowm (H4725, with H539 ne'eman) — a sure place; the security of the nail itself, not merely its bearing power.
Hebrew massa' (H4853) — a burden, a load; what the nail bears, and what falls with it when it is cut down.
usage: “all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons” — the whole household hung on one peg.
“I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place” — the security the vessels depend on.
“the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed” — the fall that takes every vessel with it.

pos: a. (uncommon; seldom found or occurring; in the Authorized Version, beyond the reach of any but God)
etymology: Latin rarus, thin, sparse, infrequent. The word measures scarcity, and Daniel's one use of it sets the scarcest possible request against the one source able to supply it.
biblical_def:
Nebuchadnezzar's demand of his wise men in Daniel two is deliberately impossible by ordinary standards: not merely to interpret a dream, but to tell the king what the dream was, without being told, on pain of death for the entire guild of Chaldeans, astrologers, and magicians if they fail. Their own answer names exactly what is being asked of them: it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. They are not wrong. It is rare — rarer than rare, a thing no merely human skill has ever supplied, and they say so honestly rather than bluff their way to an answer.

The chapter's whole force depends on what happens next. Daniel does not claim to possess the rare thing in himself; he asks for time, then prays with his three companions, and the secret is revealed to him in a night vision. His own explanation to the king matches the wise men's diagnosis exactly and then answers it: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets. The wise men were right that the thing was beyond flesh; they were wrong only in stopping there, as though rarity beyond human reach meant the matter was simply unanswerable. What is genuinely rare to men is not rare to the God who reveals secrets, and the whole point of the chapter is the difference between those two facts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): scarce; seldom happening or found; not frequent; uncommon; hence, of unusual excellence or value.
webster_full: RARE, a. Thinly scattered; hence, seldom occurring; not common; unusual; and often, of extraordinary excellence.
REQUIRE, v.t. To demand; to ask as of right and by authority; to claim as due.
REVEAL, v.t. To disclose; to make known that which was before secret or unknown, especially by supernatural means.
SECRET, n. Something studiously hidden or concealed; a matter unknown or undisclosed.
MAGICIAN, n. One skilled in magic; one who practises the black art; an enchanter.
scriptures: Dan 2:10

The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king's matter: therefore there is no king, lord, nor ruler, that asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean.
Dan 2:11
And it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.
Dan 2:28
But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;
Dan 2:47
The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.
corruption_summary: Rarity is treated as a synonym for impossibility, when Daniel's chapter uses the word precisely to set up its opposite: what is rare beyond every human resource is not rare at all to the God who reveals secrets.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; rare still names simple scarcity. The principle worth recovering is the honest half-truth in the Chaldeans' own answer — they were right that no human skill could supply the king's demand, and their fear of the sentence they had earned was entirely reasonable.

Their error was theological, not factual: they knew the gods they served did not dwell with flesh and could not be reached, and they stopped there, as though that settled the matter. Daniel's answer does not deny the rarity; it names a different God, one who does reveal secrets to flesh, and lets that difference carry the whole chapter to its end. What is genuinely rare to man remains the ordinary business of the God who is not far from any of His creatures.
roots_summary: Aramaic yaqqiyr (H3358), rare, precious, difficult; the word the wise men use of the king's demand in the Aramaic portion of Daniel.
roots_lines: Aramaic yaqqiyr (H3358) — rare, precious, difficult, weighty; the Chaldeans' own word for the king's demand.
Aramaic chakkiym (H2445) — wise, a wise man; the title of the whole guild that confesses its own limit here.
Aramaic galah (H1541) — to reveal, to uncover; the verb behind “revealeth secrets” in Daniel 2:28 and 2:47.
Aramaic raz (H7328) — a secret, a mystery; a loanword into Aramaic for exactly the kind of thing Nebuchadnezzar demanded.
Aramaic elah shemayin — the God of heaven; the title Daniel gives the one source of the rare thing the wise men could not supply.
usage: “it is a rare thing that the king requireth” — the wise men's honest confession of their limit.
“there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets” — Daniel's answer to that same limit.
“a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets” — Nebuchadnezzar's own verdict once the rare thing was shown him.

pos: a. (not credible; surpassing belief; in the Authorized Version, Paul's challenge over the resurrection of the dead)
etymology: Latin incredibilis, from in-, not, and credibilis, credible, from credere, to believe — the same root as creed and credit. What is incredible is, at root, simply what one has decided not to trust.
biblical_def:
Paul's defense before Agrippa turns on a single rhetorical question that is really the hinge of the whole book of Acts: Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead? He does not ask whether the resurrection happened — he has already staked his entire ministry on the fact that it did, in the person of Christ — he asks why the bare category, God raising the dead, should be thought impossible in the first place, when the God in question is the same one his hearers already claim to believe made the world.

The question is aimed precisely at the gap between what a man says he believes about God and what he is actually prepared to accept God can do. Agrippa and Festus both profess belief in the God of Israel; neither is willing to grant that this God could raise a dead man. Paul's word to the Corinthians makes the logic explicit: if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not risen either, and the whole faith collapses with the denial. Incredible, in Paul's mouth, is never a neutral description of what is hard to believe; it is a diagnosis of a will that has already decided, before the evidence is weighed, what a God who truly made heaven and earth is and is not allowed to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not credible; surpassing belief; too extraordinary and improbable to be believed by a rational and sensible mind.
webster_full: INCREDIBLE, a. Not to be believed; surpassing belief; too strange or improbable to obtain credit.
RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; chiefly, the revival of the dead of the human race, and their reunion with their souls.
RAISE, v.t. To lift; to elevate; to cause to rise; especially, to bring back to life from death.
BELIEVE, v.t. To be persuaded of the truth of, on the ground of evidence, testimony, or authority.
PREACH, v.t. To proclaim; to publish in religious discourse; to inculcate publicly by argument or exhortation.
scriptures: Act 26:8
Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead?
Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come:
That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.
Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?
corruption_summary: Incredible is worn as a badge of intellectual seriousness, when Paul aims the word squarely at unbelief that has already decided in advance what an almighty God is not permitted to do.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain sense of the word; what is treated as incredible has simply shifted target, from the resurrection specifically to the supernatural generally. The principle Paul names is unchanged either way: calling a thing incredible is not a neutral verdict of reason, it is a claim about what God is and is not able or willing to do.

Paul's question to Agrippa exposes the inconsistency directly — a hearer who already professes to believe in a Creator God has no coherent ground left for finding the raising of the dead uniquely incredible. First Corinthians pushes the same logic to its full weight: deny the resurrection of the dead as a category, and the resurrection of Christ falls with it, and with that denial the whole of the Christian preaching, and the whole of Christian faith, is shown to be vain.
roots_summary: Greek apistos (G571), unbelievable, faithless; the adjective behind “incredible” in Paul's question to Agrippa; anastasis (G386), resurrection, the fact in question.
roots_lines: Greek apistos (G571) — incredible, unbelieving, faithless; the same root as pistis, faith, with the negative attached.
Greek anastasis (G386) — a standing up again, resurrection; the fact Paul insists is not incredible.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to raise up, to awaken; the verb of God's own action, raising the dead.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to preach, to proclaim as a herald; the verb behind 1 Corinthians 15:12's “preached.”
Greek mataios (G3152) — vain, empty, fruitless; the word Paul uses two verses later of faith without the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:14).
usage: “Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you” — Paul's question to Agrippa and Festus.
“that God should raise the dead” — the specific fact called incredible.
“how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead” — the same denial reaching the church at Corinth.

pos: n. (grandeur; splendid display; in the Authorized Version, the glory of a goddess the gospel emptied)
etymology: Latin magnificentia, from magnus, great, and facere, to make or do — literally, great-making, the doing of great and splendid things. The Authorized Version's one use of the word belongs to Ephesus, and to an idol.
biblical_def:
Demetrius the silversmith gathers the craftsmen of Ephesus against Paul with an argument that names its real stakes without embarrassment: their trade is threatened, and beyond the trade, that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth. The magnificence in question was real by any worldly measure — the temple of Artemis at Ephesus was counted one of the wonders of the ancient world, and the city's wealth and identity were bound up in it. Demetrius is not exaggerating the splendor; he is exactly right about how much of it the gospel was putting at risk.

What makes the verse worth keeping is how little the text argues back on Demetrius's own terms. Luke does not deny Diana's magnificence was impressive; he simply lets the riot run its course, lets the town clerk quiet the crowd with a plea for order rather than a theological rebuttal, and moves on to Paul's departure for Macedonia. The silversmiths were right that a great magnificence was under threat, and the book of Acts treats that as no argument at all for its preservation. Splendor built around an idol is still splendor built around an idol, however many centuries it has stood and however much of Asia bows down to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): grandeur of appearance; splendor; greatness of show or state, as in buildings, decorations, or works of art.
webster_full: MAGNIFICENCE, n. Grandeur of show; splendor; the state of being magnificent, as in buildings, dress, equipage or decorations.
DESPISE, v.t. To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to look upon with contempt as mean and worthless.
CRAFT, n. A trade or occupation requiring skill; also, the persons engaged in such a trade, collectively.
WORSHIP, v.t. To pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration.
TUMULT, n. The commotion or agitation of a multitude; violent commotion or excitement of a crowd, attended with confused clamor.
scriptures: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
corruption_summary: Magnificence is treated as its own justification, worthy of preservation simply for its scale and antiquity, when Acts sets Diana's magnificence directly against the gospel and never once concedes that the scale of the idol is a reason to spare it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word; splendor is still splendor. The principle worth recovering is Luke's flat refusal to argue with Demetrius on his own terms. The silversmith's case for Diana is entirely about magnitude — the size of the temple, the reach of her worship across Asia, the money the trade brought in — and none of it is treated in Acts as a reason the gospel should slow down.

The riot that follows shows exactly how much force magnificence can generate in its own defense: a whole city shouting the same line for two hours, a trade's income and a goddess's honor fused into one cry. Scripture's answer is not a counter-argument about aesthetics but a plain refusal to be impressed — the true measure of any magnificence is not its size or its worshippers' numbers but whether it magnifies the true God or an idol made with hands.
roots_summary: Greek megaleiotes (G3168), majesty, magnificence, greatness; the word Demetrius applies to Diana, elsewhere used of the majesty of the true God.
roots_lines: Greek megaleiotes (G3168) — magnificence, majesty; the very word applied to God's own greatness in Luke 9:43 and 2 Peter 1:16.
Greek naos (G3485) — a temple, a sanctuary; the building whose magnificence Demetrius fears losing.
Greek sebomai (G4576) — to worship, to reverence; the verb behind “worshippeth” applied here to Diana.
Greek techne (G5078) — a craft, an art, a trade; the root of Demetrius's own occupation and complaint.
Greek ergasia (G2039) — gain, profit, business; the real interest running underneath the appeal to the goddess's honor.
usage: “that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed” — Demetrius's alarm.
“Great is Diana of the Ephesians” — the crowd's answering cry.
“a worshipper of the great goddess Diana” — the town clerk's own description of the city's identity.
